verdict: Avoid new tea plantation exposure in Nilgiris; only lend to vertically-linked, low-leverage estates with hard collateral and monthly cash sweeps.
title: Nilgiris Tea Plantations: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Nilgiris tea estate is a factory attached to a slow biological asset: bushes are plucked, leaf is withered, rolled, fermented and fired within hours, and made tea is sold at auction or to a buyer.** Cash arrives after the sale and the buyer's credit period, while wages, fuel and fertiliser go out every week, so the working-capital cycle is permanently negative for the grower. **Value sits in bush age and yield, not in the land title** — ICRA notes one peer's favourable age profile, with around 82% of bushes in the 6-50 year group in FY2026, giving a yield of 2,370 kg/hectare [8]. **Capex is replanting and factory machinery, both lumpy and deferrable, which is exactly why weak estates stop replanting and quietly run down.**

## What has changed now
**The local demand signal is weak: Tamil Nadu GST collections are -3.2% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, a 9.3 pp gap [D].** Nationally, exports are -13.6% Apr-to-date in USD [D], and tea is an export-exposed commodity, so auction realisations carry the risk.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue estates with a captive buyer or a brand, not pure auction sellers.** KDHP works because 18% of FY2026 tea goes to TCPL, which holds 28.5% and leases the gardens to it [9]; TSAIL works because Rs 65.68 crore of liquid investments as on 31 March 2026 kept net debt negative [8]. **So when a proposal lands, check the share of output sold to a named buyer on contract; if it is under a third, ask who absorbs the auction price swing.** Avoid single-garden proprietorships with no replanting record and no buyer tie.

## How to grow safely
**Structure as a cash-credit against auction receivables and warehouse stock, with a term loan only for replanting, never for working capital.** Take a monthly stock-and-receivable statement, monthly wage and fuel payout, and the auction sale statement every month. **Covenant on debt-service cover and on bush-age profile; if replanting falls below the estate's own normal rate, ask why before renewing.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch rainfall and road access: a timber lorry rolled into a tea estate near Kotagiri after rain-soaked roadside soil gave way [2] — slope failure damages bushes and blocks leaf movement to the factory.** A missed wage week, leaf diverted to bought-leaf factories, or a shift from contract to open auction sale are the first real signals.
watch: realisation below estate's own trailing average for two months -> cut drawing power
wage payment delayed past the estate's normal date -> stop fresh disbursal
receivables ageing beyond the buyer's stated credit period -> ask for buyer confirmation
access road blocked or bush damage reported -> inspect estate before renewal
